routes.description: Emergent spacetime, irreducible consciousness, and the mental character of experience are offered as convergent evidence for a fundamental conscious source called God.
routes.successCriteria: Show that the cited evidence is better explained by fundamental consciousness than by nonconscious alternatives and that the inferred mind warrants the God designation.

motionBridge.description: A fundamental conscious source best explains spacetime, matter, and contingent minds and therefore supports God's existence.

centralBridges.description: The structures underlying emergent spacetime possess sufficiently mind-like properties to favor a conscious foundation.
Consciousness is irreducible to matter, while physical reality is intelligible as the representation or content of mind.
Metaphysical conclusions may be supported defeasibly through inference to the best explanation from available evidence.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Scientific consensus and methodological naturalism cannot alone exclude minority or metaphysical interpretations.
Calling the inferred fundamental conscious source God is a concluding label rather than an assumed premise.

routes.description: The evidence is said to underdetermine theism because nonconscious pantheist or natural explanations fit it, while ultimate divine properties exceed current human justification.
routes.successCriteria: Establish that the pro evidence fails to discriminate for consciousness or divine properties and that naturalistic or agnostic alternatives retain equal or better support.

motionBridge.description: Evidence compatible with equally adequate non-theistic alternatives does not indicate God or make theism preferable.

centralBridges.description: Naturalistic pantheism functions as a countermodel showing that the cited observations do not uniquely favor theism.
Current human knowledge cannot justify ultimate metaphysical stopping points or unrestricted divine attributes.
The repeated success of natural explanation provides defeasible reason to prefer an unknown natural cause over a novel ontology.
Neural dependence evidence challenges treating consciousness correlations differently from other brain-mediated functions.

subsidiaryBridges.description: A nonpersonal foundation posits fewer properties than an omnipotent, conscious, morally perfect personal being.
Involuntary suffering counts against the existence of an all-good and all-powerful God.

sections.title: Emergent spacetime and discriminating evidence
sections.rationale: This section contains the affirmative's principal mind-from-emergence inference and the negative's strongest parsimony and nonconscious-model objections.

sections.title: Idealist ontology and the moral countercase
sections.rationale: These independent central considerations test the affirmative's mental ontology and the negative's challenge to an omnibenevolent creator.

sections.title: Metaphysical knowledge and burden
sections.rationale: The exchange directly tests whether the negative's restriction on metaphysical justification is self-undermining or properly limited to present evidence.

sections.title: Method, consensus, and natural induction
sections.rationale: This section preserves the decisive dispute over methodological assumptions, expert consensus, arguments from ignorance, and defeasible naturalistic induction.

sections.title: Natural theology and pantheist countermodel
sections.rationale: The paired Q&A statements clarify both the affirmative's evidence-first God inference and the negative's use of pantheism solely as an underdetermining countermodel.

sections.title: Neural correlations and conscious agency
sections.rationale: The final exchange supplies the most developed empirical challenge to irreducible consciousness and the affirmative's non-dualist idealist answer.

moves.proposition: Because spacetime and matter emerge from quantum structures also used to model cognition, a mind is the simplest explanation of the universe's underlying source.
moves.attributionBasis: Jones states this continuously during his assigned opening and explicitly draws the inference from shared quantum or Hilbert-space properties to a mind.

response.rationale: This is an opening constructive with no earlier selected target and directly launches the affirmative's principal route from emergent spacetime to mind.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is recoverable, but resemblance, indistinguishability, and simplicity shift without a criterion specifying which properties are explanatory.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Shared formal modeling and spacetime emergence establish compatibility, but do not by themselves make a cosmic mind the most likely source.

charity.alternative: No live alternative is represented within this constructive span.
charity.decisiveQualification: Charity is therefore not tested for this move.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The route is intelligible, but the bridge from shared mathematical structures to ontological mentality remains materially unsupported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The cited emergence and cognition claims are relevant, yet their conjunction does not establish identity or comparative explanatory superiority.

responsiveness.rationale: As a constructive opening, it clearly advances the central affirmative case without needing to answer an earlier target.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the complete motion-level conclusion by identifying the proposed conscious foundation of reality.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move does not represent or attack a live alternative, so the closed charity anchor is exactly seventy-five.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 300–325 supply the emergence, quantum-cognition, resemblance, and parsimony claims in Jones's opening argument.

moves.proposition: Conscious experience does not reduce to matter, experienced physical qualities are mental, and rejecting substance dualism therefore favors a single mental reality governed by a larger mind.
moves.attributionBasis: Jones explicitly introduces his third argument, develops the irreducibility and anti-dualist premises, and concludes that all is mind within one uninterrupted opening turn.

response.rationale: The move independently constructs the affirmative's idealist route and has no earlier selected objection that it purports to answer.

precisionFindings.rationale: The argument is recoverable, but mind, mental phenomena, substance, and physical reality are not defined with enough stability to secure the conclusion.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The hard problem and the mental presentation of qualities support explanatory difficulty for materialism, not the necessary conclusion that all reality is mind.

charity.alternative: Materialism explains experience through brain processes, while substance dualism treats mind and matter as distinct interacting substances.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move notes correlation rather than production but does not engage stronger emergent or identity-based materialist accounts.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument has a recognizable progression, but rejecting reduction and dualism does not exhaust the available ontological alternatives.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Neural correlation and phenomenal character motivate the problem, while the governing-mind conclusion receives little independent comparative support.

responsiveness.rationale: The constructive clearly advances an adopted central burden and develops multiple premises rather than merely asserting idealism.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially advances the central idealist-consciousness bridge, though it does not independently complete the motion-level God inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: Materialism is reduced largely to an emergence claim and confusion of correlation with causation, omitting its stronger theoretical qualifications.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 439–484 state the correlation objection, phenomenal-quality argument, anti-dualist premise, and conclusion that reality is mind.

moves.proposition: Evidence does not indicate God when it is explained equally well by a necessary but mindless naturalistic pantheism, whether the affirmative arguments are considered separately or together.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator gives Jump the second opening, and Jump then introduces the rabbit-box criterion and applies it continuously to theism and pantheism.

response.rationale: Although contrary to earlier affirmative material, this span opens Jump's own governing evidential case rather than performing component-level rebuttal of one selected move.

precisionFindings.rationale: The evidential criterion, the countermodel's mindlessness, and the separate-and-collective scope of the challenge are all stated explicitly.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Equal fit would defeat discrimination, but the opening initially asserts rather than fully demonstrates equal explanatory adequacy for every cited argument.

charity.alternative: Theism treats the arguments collectively as abductive evidence for a conscious and personal ultimate source.
charity.decisiveQualification: Jump expressly includes the cumulative version rather than attacking only isolated arguments.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The countermodel test is coherent and applies consistently, with the remaining issue being whether equal adequacy is actually established.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The analogy clarifies evidential discrimination, but equivalence between the full theories requires more property-by-property comparative demonstration.

responsiveness.rationale: As the negative's constructive opening, it clearly supplies an opposing motion-level criterion and countermodel.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the negative motion bridge that the affirmative evidence fails to indicate God.

representationalCharity.rationale: It accurately recognizes both individual and cumulative abductive forms of the affirmative case and preserves their intended conclusion.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 512–557 define the evidential standard, identify mindless pantheism, and apply equal compatibility to individual and cumulative arguments.

moves.proposition: Present human knowledge cannot justify ultimate metaphysical stopping points, so assigning uncreated or unlimited properties to God can be mirrored by alternatives and indicates none of them.
moves.attributionBasis: Jump advances this thesis in his uninterrupted opening, explaining stopping points and applying the restriction to divine and pantheist properties.

response.rationale: This is a distinct constructive epistemic route with no selected earlier target and supplies the warrant for withholding ultimate metaphysical conclusions.

precisionFindings.rationale: Stopping point and justification are explained, but the initial universal wording is only later restricted clearly to current limited human knowledge.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Underdetermination supports caution about final attributes, but the categorical claim that no known knowledge can justify any such property exceeds the supplied demonstration.

charity.alternative: Theistic arguments infer an uncreated, necessary, or perfect source as the best explanation rather than merely defining those properties into existence.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move focuses on definitional stopping points and does not fully address defeasible abductive support short of absolute proof.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The regress and symmetry concern is intelligible, but the move blurs absolute proof with weaker evidential justification.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Examples establish possible undiscovered alternatives, while possibility alone does not show that every comparative metaphysical inference lacks support.

responsiveness.rationale: As a constructive opening, it develops a substantial independent negative route concerning the limits of ultimate explanation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move strongly advances the negative's central epistemic-limits bridge without itself proving the entire motion-level conclusion.

representationalCharity.rationale: It treats divine-property inferences mainly as unsupported definitions and omits their claimed abductive or deductive warrants.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 577–635 define metaphysical stopping points, invoke undiscovered higher alternatives, and apply the objection to divine attributes.

moves.proposition: Pantheism is explanatorily simpler because it posits fewer properties than a personal, conscious, omniscient, and morally perfect God, and unlimited power is not itself simplicity.
moves.attributionBasis: Jump states this property comparison continuously in his opening and explicitly contrasts the restricted pantheist foundation with the less restricted theistic one.

components.text: A mind is the simplest explanation of the universe's underlying source.
Shared quantum-model properties support identifying the source as mind-like.

response.rationale: The move directly attacks m01's decisive simplicity claim through a property comparison, but it does not answer the separate resemblance inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparison is clear, but explanatory simplicity is treated mainly as a count of listed properties without resolving dependence among attributes.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Fewer independent properties can favor parsimony, but the move assumes without fully defending that all listed divine attributes add separate complexity.

charity.alternative: Divine simplicity holds that apparently multiple attributes are entailed by or identical with one noncomposite divine nature.
charity.decisiveQualification: Jump acknowledges the entailment response but treats it as arbitrary rather than developing its strongest metaphysical rationale.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The comparative route is coherent, though simple property counting leaves a material bridge about independence and theoretical cost.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The explicit comparison is useful, but no general model-selection warrant establishes that fewer verbal predicates always means greater simplicity.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts the decisive parsimony component of m01 but leaves the mind-resemblance component unanswered.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move attacks a necessary subsidiary parsimony bridge within the affirmative's emergence route.

representationalCharity.rationale: It mentions the strongest divine-simplicity qualification but dismisses it too quickly as definitional or arbitrary.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 703–734 contrast restricted and unrestricted explanations, enumerate properties, and acknowledge the divine-entailment response.

moves.proposition: An all-good and all-powerful God would prevent involuntary coercion, because any good served by suffering could be offered voluntarily in a morally better world.
moves.attributionBasis: Jump explicitly introduces this as his final opening point and continuously states both the consent-based standard and the answer to sufficient-reason defenses.

response.rationale: This is an independent negative constructive against an omnibenevolent and omnipotent God, not a response to an earlier selected component.

precisionFindings.rationale: The consent standard is explicit, but all suffering and coercion are treated together without qualifications for agency, prevention, or logically connected goods.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The voluntary-world proposal creates a serious challenge, but it does not establish that every possible morally sufficient reason could remain available unchanged.

charity.alternative: A theodicy may hold that permitting suffering is logically connected to freedom, development, stable laws, or goods unavailable on purely optional terms.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move answers these collectively by asserting optional availability, without testing whether some goods logically require nonoptional risk.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument has a clear moral comparison, but the universal optionality premise remains a substantial unsupported bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceivable consent-preserving world is relevant, yet no support shows that it preserves every allegedly justifying good.

responsiveness.rationale: As an independent constructive, it clearly states and supports a negative consideration concerning the divine attributes at issue.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It supports the negative's subsidiary moral objection but does not address a necessary premise of every possible God concept.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move identifies sufficient-reason theodicies but compresses diverse versions into an unestablished claim that their goods can always be optional.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 787–812 state the consent-preserving world, anticipate sufficient-reason replies, and assert that their goods could be made optional.

moves.proposition: Emergent spacetime does not entail mind, because the relevant models permit nonconscious underlying conditions and consciousness-collapse interpretations lack broad specialist acceptance.
moves.attributionBasis: Despite rapid unlabeled alternation, the sustained rebuttal to Jones's opening and the ensuing consensus exchange identify Jump as the speaker; the recorded medium attribution remains binding.

components.text: Emergent spacetime and quantum cognition jointly favor a mental source.
A mind is the simplest explanation of the underlying source.

response.rationale: Together with the selected section's property comparison, this move directly denies that emergence supplies consciousness and gives a nonconscious model plus expert rejection against the inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The physical emergence claim, added consciousness inference, nonconscious alternative, and limited consensus point are distinguishable and recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Compatibility with nonconscious models defeats entailment, but atheistic physicists and minority status do not prove the mental interpretation false.

charity.alternative: Jones infers mind philosophically from the properties of the underlying structure rather than claiming that emergence alone explicitly contains consciousness.
charity.decisiveQualification: Jump separates the model from the added inference but sometimes treats expert atheism as if it directly refuted that philosophical bridge.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The core distinction between physical emergence and an added mental inference is sound, with consensus functioning only as secondary support.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A nonconscious model and Wigner's reported reversal are pertinent, though speaker worldview and consensus are not dispositive evidence.

responsiveness.rationale: The response contacts the decisive emergence-to-mind inference and the connected simplicity claim, albeit with an overreliance on authority.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central bridge that emergent spacetime supplies evidence for a conscious foundation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move substantially captures Jones's inference but occasionally compresses it into the weaker claim that emergence by itself entails mind.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 881–915 distinguish emergent spacetime from mind, cite nonconscious natural conditions, specialist consensus, and Wigner's reported rejection.

moves.proposition: Saying that no human knowledge can justify metaphysical absolutes risks becoming an unsupported absolute restriction unless its evidential basis and limited scope are defended.
moves.attributionBasis: The rapid exchange contains both voices, but Jones clearly supplies the self-undermining challenge while Jump's qualification begins within the inclusive candidate span.

components.text: No known form of human knowledge can justify ultimate metaphysical stopping points.
Divine properties can therefore be mirrored by alternatives and support none.

response.rationale: Jones attacks the decisive scope and consistency of m04's epistemic restriction, but does not address the separate countermodel symmetry argument.

precisionFindings.rationale: The self-reference objection is clear, but absolute alternates between universal metaphysical truth and a strong statement about current human justification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Framed as a risk unless defended, the force appropriately matches the ambiguity in Jump's initial universal wording.

charity.alternative: Jump's claim is epistemic and limited to presently available human forms of knowledge, not a metaphysical assertion about all possible knowledge.
charity.decisiveQualification: The candidate span includes Jump beginning this restriction, which materially weakens a simple self-contradiction charge.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The challenge is coherent against the broad wording, but loses force once epistemic and metaphysical modalities are distinguished.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The quoted universal language supports scrutiny, though it does not alone establish that the statement is itself a metaphysical absolute.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts the decisive scope component of m04 while leaving the independent symmetry and underdetermination component unanswered.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the negative's central epistemic-limits bridge by challenging its consistency and support.

representationalCharity.rationale: Jones initially omits the available current-human-knowledge qualification, though the exchange allows Jump to state it.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 1097–1122 contain the absolute-claim objection, Jump's current-human-knowledge qualification, and Jones's shift toward probability.

moves.proposition: The restriction denies that current evidence justifies an ultimate metaphysical claim; it does not declare the claim metaphysically false or impossible, and the claimant retains the justificatory burden.
moves.attributionBasis: Although the span contains rapid back-and-forth speech, Jump repeatedly articulates the epistemic-versus-metaphysical distinction and invokes the claimant's burden.

components.text: The epistemic restriction is itself an unsupported metaphysical absolute.
The restriction requires an evidential defense and appropriately limited scope.

response.rationale: Jump directly distinguishes present justification from metaphysical falsity and supplies a burden-based rationale, contacting both components of Jones's challenge.

precisionFindings.rationale: Current human evidence, justification, metaphysical falsity, possibility, and the claimant's burden are expressly distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modal distinction is secure, but the further certainty that no current human evidence can justify the claim still requires broader support.

charity.alternative: Jones treats metaphysical claims as defeasible best explanations rather than assertions requiring absolute proof.
charity.decisiveQualification: Jump preserves the distinction between falsity and nonjustification but continues to use justification more strictly than Jones does.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The epistemic-modal distinction defeats the simple self-contradiction objection, though it does not itself prove the broad evidential restriction.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The burden distinction is well supported conceptually, while the universal claim about all current human evidence remains compressed.

responsiveness.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive self-reference objection and states why the limited claim does not entail metaphysical impossibility.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The answer restores the central negative bridge by clarifying its intended epistemic rather than metaphysical scope.

representationalCharity.rationale: It fairly distinguishes Jones's metaphysical assertion from proof, but underrepresents his weaker best-explanation standard.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 1186–1218 repeatedly distinguish nonjustification from falsity, restrict the claim to current epistemic resources, and discuss burden.

moves.proposition: Methodological naturalism is a prior philosophical shaping principle because the scientific method cannot establish its own authority solely through its operation.
moves.attributionBasis: Jones sustains the self-validation argument immediately before Jump's contrary response, clearly identifying the affirmative speaker despite unlabeled dialogue.

response.rationale: The selected span constructs a distinct philosophy-of-science objection and does not purport to answer a particular earlier selected move component.

precisionFindings.rationale: The self-validation concern is clear, but assumption shifts between an unavoidable starting rule and an empirically unsupported absolute commitment.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A method cannot noncircularly prove itself with certainty, but it may still acquire defeasible inductive justification from demonstrated success.

charity.alternative: Methodological naturalism is a revisable practice justified instrumentally and inductively by successful operation rather than an absolute metaphysical axiom.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move anticipates neither revisability nor the distinction between self-proof and evidence of reliability.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The regress concern is intelligible, but inability to prove a method absolutely does not entail that it is merely assumed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The philosophy-of-science point supports fallibilism, while the stronger metaphysical-shaping conclusion receives limited warrant.

responsiveness.rationale: As a constructive methodological move, it clearly advances a subsidiary affirmative burden without an earlier required target.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It supports the subsidiary claim that scientific method alone cannot exclude metaphysical interpretations.

representationalCharity.rationale: It reconstructs methodological naturalism as an assumed absolute and omits its strongest pragmatic and inductive justification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 1695–1712 state the self-validation problem and characterize methodological naturalism as an assumed philosophical shaping principle.

moves.proposition: Methodological naturalism need not be assumed as absolutely true, because trying the method and observing repeated success supplies inductive reason to continue using it.
moves.attributionBasis: The move immediately denies Jones's preceding assertion and develops Jump's success-based inductive justification in the alternating exchange.

components.text: The scientific method cannot establish itself through its own operation.
Methodological naturalism must therefore be assumed as a metaphysical shaping principle.

response.rationale: Jump answers both the self-validation demand and metaphysical-assumption conclusion by replacing absolute proof with demonstrated, defeasible inductive success.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly distinguishes assumption, demonstration, induction, successful operation, and good reason from absolute self-proof.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Repeated methodological success appropriately supplies defeasible rather than certain support for continued reliance.

charity.alternative: Jones argues that a method cannot validate its own authority without already employing contested methodological standards.
charity.decisiveQualification: Jump accepts that the support is inductive, thereby preserving the strongest limited form of Jones's circularity concern.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The response coherently distinguishes absolute validation from fallible inductive justification and avoids the alleged regress.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Observed success is an appropriate warrant for instrumental reliance, with only the breadth and definition of success left compressed.

responsiveness.rationale: It directly contacts both indispensable components and supplies the precise defeasible alternative missing from m10.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move defeats a necessary subsidiary methodological bridge rather than independently completing the negative motion burden.

representationalCharity.rationale: It preserves Jones's point that induction is involved while accurately denying that this makes the method an absolute metaphysical assumption.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 1713–1722 explicitly distinguish trying a method, demonstrated success, inductive argument, and good reason to rely on it.

moves.proposition: Jones's three scientific and introspective arguments do not establish mind because specialists reject the proposed interpretations and an undiscovered physical cause is more parsimonious than a new ontological category.
moves.attributionBasis: Jump explicitly enumerates the digital-physics, Wigner, and introspection arguments and states the expert and parsimony objections in one rebuttal turn.

components.text: Emergent spacetime and cognition modeling favor a mental cosmic source.
Consciousness cannot reduce to matter and therefore supports idealism.
Rejecting substance dualism helps establish that all reality is mind.

response.rationale: The rebuttal contacts the decisive empirical inferences in both earlier affirmative routes, but it does not address m02's anti-dualist elimination step.

precisionFindings.rationale: The three targets and two rebuttal strategies are identifiable, though wrong sometimes conflates scientific disagreement with inferential failure.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Consensus and naturalistic induction weaken the affirmative interpretations but do not establish their falsity or the superior physical explanation with certainty.

charity.alternative: Jones presents positive deductive or abductive arguments from emergence, collapse interpretations, and phenomenal irreducibility rather than inferring God solely from ignorance.
charity.decisiveQualification: The rebuttal labels introspection an ignorance argument without first addressing its stated positive premises.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The rival-explanation strategy is coherent, but expert rejection and historical induction do not alone prove the affirmative evidence wrong.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specialist disagreement, Wigner's reported reversal, and naturalistic track record are relevant but incompletely documented and compared.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts both decisive empirical components but leaves the anti-dualist premise and some affirmative warrants unanswered.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The consolidated rebuttal attacks the complete affirmative motion route across its principal scientific and consciousness arguments.

representationalCharity.rationale: Calling the introspective route an argument from ignorance omits its positive phenomenal and anti-dualist premises.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 1766–1784 enumerate the affirmative arguments, report specialist rejection, invoke Wigner, and prefer an unknown physical force.

moves.proposition: Consensus is not dispositive, the affirmative offers a positive deductive case rather than reasoning solely from ignorance, and claims that consciousness emerges from brains also require evidence.
moves.attributionBasis: Jones explicitly announces quick rebuttals and then answers Jump's consensus, ignorance, and physical-emergence objections in sequence.

components.text: Specialist rejection defeats the digital-physics and consciousness interpretations.
The introspective argument is an argument from ignorance.
An undiscovered physical cause is more parsimonious than a mental ontology.

response.rationale: Jones explicitly contacts every indispensable objection in m12, distinguishing positive inference from ignorance and demanding support for the proposed physical rival.

precisionFindings.rationale: The three rebuttal propositions are clear, though consensus is described categorically as meaning nothing rather than merely being nondispositive.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The burden and inference distinctions are sound, but calling consensus wholly irrelevant exceeds what the historical counterexamples establish.

charity.alternative: Jump offers consensus as defeasible evidence and naturalism as an induction from prior explanatory success, not merely an unsupported assertion.
charity.decisiveQualification: Jones accurately answers the ignorance label but compresses the probabilistic force of Jump's expert and inductive support.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The rebuttal correctly separates positive inference from bare ignorance and identifies a burden for the rival physical explanation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual distinctions are supported, while the wholesale dismissal of consensus and reference to failed materialist predictions remain underdeveloped.

responsiveness.rationale: The move explicitly and substantively contacts all three components of m12, including both decisive components.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It restores the affirmative's complete motion route against the consolidated negative rebuttal.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply treats the consensus appeal fairly enough but understates the independent inductive warrant behind the naturalistic rival.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 1785–1801 reject consensus as dispositive, distinguish deduction from ignorance, and demand evidence for brain-emergent consciousness.

moves.proposition: Natural theology begins with evidence and infers a metaphysical explanation; only a resulting conscious mind receives the title God, while an unconscious natural source would not.
moves.attributionBasis: In a question directed to Jones, he explains his own natural-theology method and expressly conditions the God label on reaching a conscious mind.

response.rationale: This later constructive clarification materially fixes the scope of the God conclusion and states an evidence-first method without targeting one earlier selected move.

precisionFindings.rationale: The direction of inference, conscious-mind condition, natural alternative, and limited reach beyond specifically Christian theism are clearly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move describes a conditional method and expressly allows that evidence could instead lead to a non-God natural explanation.

charity.alternative: An unconscious natural explanation may fit the evidence and, if favored, would not count as God.
charity.decisiveQualification: Jones explicitly accepts this possibility and limits natural theology to a conscious-source conclusion.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The evidence-first and conditional-label structure is coherent and avoids simply defining any first cause as God.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The methodological clarification is well supported by the stated procedure, though it does not add comparative evidence for consciousness.

responsiveness.rationale: As a constructive clarification, it materially advances the motion route by specifying what conclusion the evidence would need to support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly defines the affirmative's complete motion-level success condition and the boundary of the God inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: The live unconscious natural alternative is represented accurately and expressly allowed to defeat the God label if evidence favors it.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 2740–2757 describe evidence-first natural theology, allow an unconscious natural result, and limit the conclusion to a conscious mind called God.

moves.proposition: Naturalistic pantheism is offered as a countermodel rather than an endorsed worldview: if it fits the affirmative arguments equally well, those arguments indicate neither pantheism nor God.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator directs the question to Jump, who explicitly explains the purpose of his own pantheist alternative and reaffirms his atheist suspension of judgment.

components.text: Natural theology infers the best metaphysical explanation from evidence.
Only an evidence-supported conscious source warrants the God label.

response.rationale: Jump answers the evidence-first demand with an equally fitting nonconscious countermodel and explicitly states the defeating consequence that neither theory is indicated.

precisionFindings.rationale: The countermodel role, lack of endorsement, equal-fit condition, and agnostic conclusion about ultimate reality are all explicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conditional logic is well calibrated, although the assertion that the complete pantheist model fits equally well remains only partly demonstrated.

charity.alternative: Jones uses evidence to infer a conscious mind and does not treat every ultimate cause or natural entity as God.
charity.decisiveQualification: Jump preserves the affirmative's conscious-source condition while denying that the evidence discriminates for it.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between deploying and endorsing a countermodel is explicit, and the underdetermination consequence follows if equal fit holds.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The clarified countermodel strategy is strong, but equal adequacy across all affirmative evidence still needs fuller comparative support.

responsiveness.rationale: The move contacts both decisive components of m14 and separately states why equal fit defeats the requested inference.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the complete negative motion bridge that the evidence does not indicate God.

representationalCharity.rationale: It accurately represents the affirmative as an evidence-first conscious-source inference while challenging only its discriminatory success.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 2764–2781 explain the countermodel's purpose, deny endorsement of pantheism, and conclude that ultimate reality remains unknown.

moves.proposition: Brain measurements reveal third-person correlations and representations of mental processes but not subjective qualities themselves, leaving materialist production of consciousness unexplained.
moves.attributionBasis: Jones gives a sustained answer about brain correlations, explicitly identifies his dual-aspect idealism, and contrasts measurable activity with first-person sensations.

response.rationale: This is a developed constructive elaboration of the affirmative consciousness route and introduces the selected neural-evidence exchange without an earlier target.

precisionFindings.rationale: Correlation, representation, production, third-person measurement, and first-person qualities are distinguished clearly enough for evaluation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move claims explanatory incompleteness rather than proving materialism false, appropriately matching the hard-problem observation supplied.

charity.alternative: Materialists interpret systematic neural correlations as evidence that brain activity produces or realizes consciousness.
charity.decisiveQualification: Jones acknowledges this interpretation directly before arguing that measured activity does not display subjective qualities.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The explanatory-gap argument is coherent, although failure to observe qualities directly does not by itself decide their ontological realization.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The distinction between neural measurements and phenomenal qualities supports an explanatory challenge but not a complete idealist account.

responsiveness.rationale: As a constructive elaboration, it clearly advances the central consciousness burden with a specific empirical and conceptual distinction.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially supports the central affirmative bridge that consciousness is not reductively explained by neural matter.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move accurately states the materialist production interpretation and attacks its explanatory gap without gross caricature.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 3125–3156 describe neural patterns as third-person images, distinguish sensations from measurements, and identify the hard problem.

moves.proposition: If neural correlations support ordinary functions such as movement, speech, and perception, the idealist must explain why comparable correlations involving conscious experience receive different evidential treatment.
moves.attributionBasis: The questioning role, explicit contrast with Jones's position, and Jones's following answer support attribution to Jump, while the candidate's medium confidence remains binding.

components.text: Neural correlations do not establish that consciousness emerges from or is produced by the brain.
Measurements do not reveal subjective qualities themselves.

response.rationale: The move directly challenges the decisive evidential treatment of neural correlation but does not answer the separate claim that third-person measurement omits phenomenal qualities.

precisionFindings.rationale: The analogy between conscious correlations and motor, speech, and perceptual correlations is concrete and its requested distinction is explicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move appropriately poses an explanatory consistency challenge rather than claiming that correlation alone conclusively proves emergence.

charity.alternative: Jones accepts neural dependence but interprets the brain as a physical representation of an antecedent conscious agent.
charity.decisiveQualification: The question presses differential treatment without assuming that Jones denies all brain-function relations.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The parity challenge is coherent and forces a principled distinction between neural evidence for consciousness and other functions.
